title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: a yoga manual compares breath to a lion, an elephant and a tiger, and makes a promise worth checking
carry: the breath again — every claim checked
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: Patanjali puts a steady, easy seat first, and only then the breath. Did you settle the seat before a deep breath? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

A lion. An elephant. A tiger. Nobody tames one in an afternoon. A keeper works slowly, day after day, and even then stays careful. That's the picture a yoga manual called the Hatha Yoga Pradipika uses for the breath. Breath, it says, is to be brought under control the way those animals are, gradually. Then the same passage makes a promise and a warning side by side. This season has promised to check every claim, and that includes the claims an old text makes about itself. Today: the tamed lion, and a promise held up to the light.
screen: `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.` → `SLOWLY, DAY AFTER DAY.` → `A PROMISE AND A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First the image, here in paraphrase. As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed little by little, so the breath is controlled little by little. Otherwise, the text says, it harms the one who practices. That's blunt. A yoga manual is telling its readers that breath practice done carelessly can hurt them. Next, the promise and the warning in one verse. Done properly, it says, the practice puts an end to disease. Done improperly, it brings disease on. Then it lists what can go wrong: hiccups, breathing trouble, cough, pain in the head, the ears and the eyes. So now, every claim checked, including this one. The warning holds up well. Slow, gradual, careful: that is plain good sense for anyone trying a breathing practice, and these days hold to the same. The promise is a different matter. A claim that any practice ends every disease is one this path won't accept from any source, old or new. It's fair to say that clearly, and it's also fair to say what the text is doing. It is a teaching manual, urging its students toward patience by showing them both what they hope for and what they risk. The respectful reading takes the text seriously and still checks it. Keep the lion and the slowness. Leave the cure-all on the page. And notice how human the passage is. Its author knew students would rush. So it sends them to the animal keeper, who never hurries a tiger.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE` · `A PROMISE AND A WARNING IN ONE VERSE` · `THE WARNING HOLDS UP` · `THE CURE-ALL STAYS ON THE PAGE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tame nothing today, just befriend. Sit comfortably and let the breath move on its own. Notice its pace, the way a keeper watches an animal before ever reaching out a hand. If the breath wants to be quick, let it be quick. If it slows, let it slow. You're not training it, only getting to know it. If anything feels strained, go back to ordinary breathing. If you pray, you can hold one breath of thanks. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, breath is tamed little by little, like a lion, an elephant or a tiger. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, when a health promise sounds too big, keep the caution and check the promise. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: In hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are traditionally learned gradually from a teacher, and the Hatha Yoga Pradipika itself warns that rushing them can cause harm.

fork.setup: you're writing a yoga manual. you know your students will rush the breath practices. what do you do?
options: promise quick results so they stay.
tell them to go slowly, like taming a lion, and list what goes wrong.
fork.reveal: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika gives the lion, elephant and tiger, then names the ills that come from practice done wrong.

trapdoor: what you thought: old yoga texts treat breathing as harmless and good for everything.
what it means: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika warns that breath must be tamed slowly, like a lion, or it harms.
what a scholar hears: one verse holds both a cure-all promise and a list of ills from wrong practice, so the text is urging patience.

sources.ref: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.15 (as a lion, elephant or tiger is tamed gradually, so the breath; otherwise it harms the practitioner)

notes: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.15–2.17: confirm verse numbers and the paraphrase (lion, elephant, tiger tamed gradually; otherwise it 'kills' or harms the practitioner, softened here to 'harms'; proper practice destroys all diseases, improper practice causes them; hiccough, asthma, cough, pain in head, ears, eyes). Verse numbering differs between editions.
Science-seat line: the lesson declines the text's cure-all claim and keeps its caution. It is careful not to mock the text; a Keeper should check the tone is respectful.
